record.paper_title: Multi-D magnetohydrodynamic modelling of pulsar wind nebulae: recent progress and open questions
record.original_question: In the Crab Nebula, are the low-energy particles that produce radio synchrotron emission continuously injected as part of the pulsar wind and accelerated at the termination shock, produced and reaccelerated elsewhere in the nebula such as through turbulence or thermal-filament interactions, or a relic population from an early pulsar outburst, and how can observations or three-dimensional simulations discriminate among these scenarios?

evidence.quote: Although radio emitting particles are dominant by number in the Crab nebula, their origin is still a mystery.

The question is whether radio particles are part of the pulsar outflow, and accelerated at the TS together with high-energy emitting particles, or if they are of different origin and accelerated somewhere else in the nebula.

Three different hypotheses were then considered: radio particles are injected in the nebula as part of the pulsar outflow (case A); radio particles are uniformly distributed in the nebula, produced somewhere else, for instance in the thermal filaments, and continuously accelerated by the interaction with local turbulence (case B); radio particles are a relic population, born in a primordial outburst of the pulsar during its early life, and still present thanks to their very long lifetimes against synchrotron losses (case C).
This result should be validated in the future also in three dimensions, since the stronger mixing of the magnetic field lines could in principle allow for the relic scenario to be reconsidered.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
The Crab Nebula is a pulsar wind nebula whose broadband nonthermal emission ranges from radio to gamma-rays. The radio-emitting electrons (and positrons), which produce synchrotron radiation at radio frequencies, dominate by number the relativistic particle population in the nebula, yet their origin is not established. Three competing scenarios have been proposed:

(A) Wind injection scenario: the radio-emitting particles are continuously injected as a low-energy component of the relativistic pulsar wind and are accelerated, together with the higher-energy particles, at the wind termination shock.

(B) In situ scenario: the radio-emitting particles are produced in the body of the nebula itself (for example via mass loading or photoionization at the thermal filaments that are observed embedded in the synchrotron bubble) and are continuously (re)accelerated by interaction with the local MHD turbulence, yielding an approximately uniform spatial distribution.

(C) Relic scenario: the radio-emitting particles form a relic population, injected during an early high-power outburst of the pulsar at the time of its birth, which has survived to the present day owing to long synchrotron-loss timescales at low energies.

Within the framework of relativistic MHD modelling of the nebula (including 3D simulations that account for full magnetic-field-line mixing and turbulent dynamics inside the bubble), determine which of the three scenarios (A), (B), (C) is consistent with all available observational constraints on the Crab Nebula. In particular:

1. Identify quantitative observational diagnostics — e.g. the spatial distribution and spectrum of the radio surface brightness, polarization maps, the morphology and proper motions of the inner "wisps" at radio versus optical/X-ray wavelengths, the spectral index distribution across the radio-to-optical break, and the time variability of small-scale radio features — that can discriminate among scenarios (A), (B), and (C).

2. Determine, using full 3D relativistic MHD simulations of the nebula, whether the enhanced mixing of magnetic field lines in three dimensions (as opposed to axisymmetric 2D models) permits scenario (C) to reproduce the observed near-uniform spatial distribution of radio-emitting particles, given their synchrotron lifetimes in the simulated magnetic field.

3. Decide whether scenarios (A), (B), or (C) is the correct explanation for the origin of the radio-emitting particles in the Crab Nebula.
artifact.category_tag: Relativistic MHD of pulsar wind nebulae
artifact.status_search_result: The origin of the radio-emitting particles in the Crab Nebula remains an open problem. Subsequent 3D relativistic MHD simulations of the Crab Nebula (Porth et al. 2014; Olmi et al. 2016; and later reviews) confirm that the question is still unsettled: while the wind-injection scenario (A) appears most consistent with several diagnostics, 3D simulations have not definitively ruled out the in-situ or relic scenarios, and the issue is repeatedly identified as an open question in the literature.

status_evidence.title: Three-Dimensional Magnetohydrodynamic Simulations of the Crab Nebula
status_evidence.snippet: First 3D relativistic MHD simulations of the Crab Nebula with strong magnetisation, used to study particle acceleration and emission.
status_evidence.claim: 3D relativistic MHD simulations are now available, but they have not conclusively settled the origin of radio-emitting particles.

status_evidence.title: On the MHD modelling of the Crab Nebula radio emission
status_evidence.snippet: Investigates whether radio-emitting particles are part of the pulsar outflow accelerated at the termination shock, or have a different origin and acceleration site.
status_evidence.claim: The question of the origin of the radio-emitting particles in the Crab Nebula is explicitly framed as still unresolved.

status_evidence.title: A global model of particle acceleration at pulsar wind termination shocks
status_evidence.snippet: Models particle acceleration at the termination shock and discusses the origin of radio-emitting particles in pulsar wind nebulae.
status_evidence.claim: As of recent literature, the origin of the radio-emitting particles continues to be debated.
